newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Envoys head for Sierra Leone accord - officials.
newsitem.headline: Envoys head for Sierra Leone accord - officials.

text.p: Official envoys left Sierra Leone on Wednesday for Ivory Coast for the signing of a peace accord between the government and rebels to end more than six years of civil war, official sources said.

The sources in the office of President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah said the team included Justice Minister Solomon Berewa, army chief of staff Colonel Max Kanga and the United Nations Special envoy to Sierra Leone Berhanu Dinka.
"The men are part of the delegation for the signing of the agreement on Friday," one source said. It was not immediately clear whether Kabbah would also attend.
In Ivory Coast rebel leader Foday Sankoh told Reuters he had had "fruitful" talks with his guerrillas back in the Sierra Leone jungle on a mandate to sign the accord.
But he declined any comment on whether he actually got a mandate or if indeed there will be an accord this week, saying he has to first consult the Ivorian mediators.
"I can't say anything until the next 72 hours. I am waiting for the foreign minister and president of Ivory Coast," Sankoh said in Abidjan.
"Everything I do must be approved by the foreign minister (Amara Essy) as chairman of the peace talks," he added.

Essy, who has chaired negotiations between the government and Sankoh's Revolutionary United Front (RUF), was expected back in Abidjan on Thursday from accompanying President Henri Konan Bedie on a European visit.
Officials in Sierra Leone said last week that the plan was to sign a peace deal in Ivory Coast this Friday. There was no immediate comment from the Ivorian government.
Kabbah, who took office in March after multi-party elections ended four years of army rule, earlier threatened the military option if Sankoh did not agree to peace by December 1.

Sankoh's RUF took up arms in March 1991 in a low-level guerrilla campaign started from the border with Liberia. A coup in April 1992 by young officers unhappy with the conduct of the war failed to lead to a military solution.
Rebels who held foreign hostages for sometime succeeded in disrupting the country's mainstay bauxite, rutile, diamonds and gold mining industry by forcing foreign-owned mines to close.
By early 1995 rebels were attacking close to the capital, forcing the government to bring in mercenaries from South African firm Executive Outcomes to help the beleagured army.
The South Africans helped government forces retake the initiative in the fighting before army rulers began talks with Sankoh just before they handed power to Kabbah.
Kabbah and Sankoh extended a truce indefinitely in April during talks in Ivory Coast following Kabbah's election but failed to agree a definitive peace settlement.
Sankoh had been in Ivory Coast since then but the fragile truce came under strain with mutual accusation of violations.
Differences over the presence of foreign troops -- Nigerians, Guineans and mercenaries from a private South African security firm -- blocked progress towards a peace deal.
The civil war in Sierra Leone, a former British colony, has killed at least 10,000 people, according to official estimates.
